abstract: This paper argues that small, fine-tuned open-source large language models (specifically Meta's LLAMA family) can match or exceed the performance of large proprietary models like ChatGPT-4 on social science text classification tasks, while offering superior transparency, reproducibility, data privacy, and cost-effectiveness. The authors fine-tune LLAMA models using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and test them across three classification problems of varying difficulty. They also propose a hybrid human-AI workflow in which multiple LLMs generate candidate labels that human coders then reject rather than assign, accelerating the creation of labeled training data.
key_claims: Small, properly fine-tuned open-source LLMs (e.g., LLAMA2-7B) can achieve performance equal to or better than much larger closed-source models like ChatGPT-4 on domain-specific classification tasks.

Closed-source proprietary models pose serious risks for social science research, including lack of transparency, undisclosed version changes, data exposure, content moderation beyond researcher control, prohibitive cost at scale, and non-reproducibility.
Larger parameter models generally outperform smaller ones, but fine-tuning narrows or closes this gap.

Fine-tuning is less effective on base models that were pre-trained on larger token corpora (e.g., LLAMA-3 trained on 15T tokens is harder to re-weight than LLAMA-2 trained on 1.5T tokens), making weaker models like LLAMA2-7B easier to fine-tune to high performance.

A hybrid workflow using proprietary and open models for initial labeling plus human rejection of incorrect labels is faster and more efficient than traditional human coding, leveraging cognitive tendencies (error salience, negativity bias) that make detecting wrong labels easier than selecting correct ones.
methods: Fine-tuning of Meta LLAMA models (versions 2, 3, 3.1, 3.2; sizes from 1B to 405B) using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA).

A proposed five-step workflow: (1) data normalization into tabular form, (2) AI-crowd classification by multiple LLMs, (3) human approval by rejecting inapplicable labels, (4) fine-tuning a single LLM on the human-filtered set, (5) scaling to unseen documents.

Evaluation across three datasets: (i) 10,000 English tweets classified along 46 Human Flourishing Program well-being dimensions (multi-label, noisy, no gold standard), (ii) European Parliament questions (1994-2021) classified into 19 Comparative Agendas Project policy areas (mutually exclusive, gold standard exists), and (iii) Harvard Dataverse datasets classified into 15 subject categories (multi-label, highly curated, large training set of 76,110 records).

Use of multiple evaluation metrics: accuracy, precision, recall/sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, macro balanced accuracy, F1 score, Hamming loss, and Jaccard index, chosen according to task type.
Three prompting strategies for the CAP task (direct, zero-shot, and a 20-call iterative method) and comparison of fine-tuned LLAMA2-7B against base LLAMA2 models and ChatGPT-4.
Human verification by trained master's/doctoral students; inter-coder reliability assessed via Cohen's/Fleiss kappa (66.4 on a subset of parliamentary questions).
findings: On the Human Flourishing tweet task, performance improved with model size and with fine-tuning; fine-tuned LLAMA2-7B achieved results comparable to or better than ChatGPT-4 across accuracy, Hamming loss, and Jaccard index, with fine-tuning less effective for base models pre-trained on more tokens.

On the CAP policy classification task, zero-shot ChatGPT-4 and base LLAMA2-7B scored poorly (~37% accuracy), the iterative ChatGPT-4 method reached ~75.8%, and fine-tuning LLAMA2-7B raised zero-shot accuracy from ~37% to ~75% (test), with macro balanced accuracy of ~86.4-86.5% versus 83.4% for ChatGPT-4.
Certain CAP categories (Law and Crime, Regional/Urban issues, Banking/Finance) had low sensitivity, with Banking/Finance frequently misclassified as Macroeconomics.

On the Harvard Dataverse task, a fine-tuned LLAMA2-7B trained on only 5,000 labeled records matched the base 70B model (~84.8% vs 84.9% accuracy); extending the training set to 76,110 records raised accuracy to 94.6%.
The large fine-tuned Dataverse model predicted the exact correct categories (and count) 90.3% of the time, and sometimes proposed additional plausible categories beyond the original single labels.
Human coders disagree in roughly 15-20% of cases, and human annotation reliability (traditionally the 'gold standard') is increasingly questioned in the literature.
contributions: Empirical demonstration that fine-tuned small open-source LLMs are not merely 'last resort' tools but can equal or surpass large black-box models, supporting reproducible and cost-effective social science research.
A reusable five-step hybrid human-AI workflow for accelerating labeled dataset creation, grounded in cognitive principles of error detection.
An empirical observation linking fine-tuning efficacy to base-model pre-training corpus size, suggesting less-trained models are easier to specialize.
Evaluation across three contrasting real-world social science classification tasks spanning noisy/unlabeled data, gold-standard political data, and highly curated metadata.
A practical pathway for large-scale analyses (e.g., Harvard's 10B Geo-Tweet archive) that would be financially infeasible with commercial API pricing, using locally deployable open models.
framing: The paper positions itself within computational social science and the open-versus-closed foundation model debate, engaging methodological concerns about replicability, transparency, data privacy, and scalability in LLM-based text classification. It responds to prior work (e.g., Barrie & Spirling, Palmer et al.) that frames open models as replicability-preserving but inferior, arguing instead that fine-tuned open models can be both reproducible and high-performing.
